submission.name: RideKind
submission.tagline: Find a shared ride that fits your route and your footprint.
submission.inspiration: Long trips to campus events and weekend meetups can be expensive when everyone drives alone. We wanted a simple way for students heading in similar directions to find each other and make carpooling feel practical.
submission.what_it_does: RideKind lets a driver post a trip and lets riders look for trips by destination, timing, and vehicle type. It shows possible matches with a rough emissions comparison to help people consider sharing the ride.
submission.how_we_built_it: We sketched the trip and match screens in Figma, then built a React interface for searching and posting rides. A small Python backend stores trip details and handles matching; we planned to use Databricks to prepare trip and distance data for the emissions view, but that part did not connect to the full demo.
submission.challenges_we_ran_into: We lost time settling on the project, which left less time for wiring the pieces together. The ride screens and backend routes run in isolation, but posting a trip through to a complete match did not work reliably, and our analytics view stayed unfinished.
submission.accomplishments: We made a usable set of ride search and posting screens and got the basic backend pieces running. We also defined a first pass at matching around route, timing, and vehicle details.
submission.what_we_learned: We learned that even a simple matching feature depends on consistent trip data and clear assumptions about what counts as a useful match. Working with Databricks also showed us that analytics needs a prepared dataset and a working path back to the interface.
submission.whats_next: We would connect trip creation, search, and match results into one dependable flow. Then we would finish the Databricks emissions summary and add clearer pickup coordination.
